abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for understanding information propagation dynamics in social web networks, fundamentally departing from traditional cascade models. Current approaches treat information diffusion as independent propagation events, failing to capture the complex interplay between semantic relevance and network topology. We propose the Semantic-Topological Co-evolution Model (STCM), which models the joint evolution of semantic content and network structure through coupled differential equations. Our framework introduces three key innovations: (1) a semantic proximity measure derived from linked data graphs that captures conceptual relationships beyond lexical similarity, (2) a dynamic rewiring mechanism where network edges form and dissolve based on content relevance, and (3) theoretical proofs demonstrating that the system exhibits phase transitions characteristic of critical phenomena in complex networks. Extensive analysis on a large-scale social web dataset comprising 2.3 million users and 180 million interactions validates our theoretical predictions. The STCM provides a new paradigm for web mining research by revealing that information diffusion and network evolution are not separate processes but unified phenomena governed by the same underlying principles. This work opens new directions for understanding emergent behavior in web-based social systems.

Existing theoretical analyses of web search ranking algorithms suffer from limiting assumptions that render them impractical for real-world applications. This paper presents a significantly improved theoretical framework for understanding and predicting the performance of learning-to-rank algorithms in web search contexts. We extend the widely-adopted click model theory by introducing a novel position-based click model with attention decay (PCMAD) that accounts for heterogeneous user behavior across different query types. Our theoretical analysis establishes tighter regret bounds for online learning algorithms operating under PCMAD, demonstrating an O(√T) improvement over existing O(log T) bounds under realistic browsing assumptions. We prove that the improved bounds are tight by constructing adversarial query sequences that achieve these lower limits. Furthermore, we derive new theoretical conditions under which counterfactual learning methods for web data management achieve finite-sample guarantees, resolving an open problem in the field. Experiments on three large-scale web search datasets validate that algorithms designed using our theoretical improvements consistently outperform state-of-the-art methods by 8-15% in NDCG scores. This work provides rigorous theoretical foundations for developing more effective web search systems.

We present DecentralWeb, a groundbreaking decentralized web architecture that fundamentally reimagines data ownership and interoperability in web applications. Existing centralized architectures create single points of failure, privacy vulnerabilities, and vendor lock-in, while prior decentralized attempts have failed to achieve mainstream adoption due to scalability and usability challenges. DecentralWeb introduces three core architectural innovations: (1) a hierarchical sharding mechanism that distributes semantic web data across federated nodes while maintaining global query consistency, (2) a novel consensus protocol specifically designed for web workloads that achieves sub-second finality with minimal energy consumption, and (3) a user-centric identity framework enabling portable digital identities across web services without centralized intermediaries. Our system implements the complete semantic web stack including RDF, SPARQL, and OWL reasoning, ensuring semantic interoperability with existing linked data infrastructure. We deployed DecentralWeb across a network of 500 nodes spanning three continents, demonstrating linear scalability to over 100 million triples while maintaining query latencies under 50ms. Security analysis confirms robust protection against Sybil attacks and data tampering. DecentralWeb represents a paradigm shift toward a web ecosystem where users maintain sovereign control over their data while enjoying the benefits of a globally interconnected information space.

This paper presents StreamMiner, a high-performance system for real-time web mining on streaming data that dramatically improves upon existing solutions. Current stream processing systems for web analytics face a fundamental trade-off between latency and accuracy, forcing practitioners to choose between near-instantaneous but approximate results or accurate but delayed insights. StreamMiner overcomes this limitation through three key system innovations: (1) an adaptive sampling framework that dynamically adjusts processing granularity based on query importance and data velocity, (2) a novel approximate aggregation engine supporting complex multi-dimensional web analytics queries with provable error bounds, and (3) an intelligent load shedding mechanism that prioritizes critical metrics during peak load conditions. The system achieves sub-second latency for 99% of queries while maintaining aggregate errors below 2%, representing a 10x improvement over the best existing approaches. StreamMiner incorporates comprehensive support for web performance monitoring, including page load time analysis, resource prioritization, and real-time anomaly detection. We deployed and evaluated the system on production web traffic from a major e-commerce platform, processing over 500,000 events per second across 15 data centers. Results demonstrate that StreamMiner enables real-time decision-making for web optimization that was previously impossible, reducing page load times by 23% through immediate identification and remediation of performance bottlenecks.
